title: Tree edit distance versus APSP
formal:
Are general weighted ordered tree edit distance and all-pairs shortest paths equivalent under deterministic subcubic reductions? With the precise problems and reduction relation defined below, the historical target is
\[
\mathrm{TED}\le_{\mathrm{sc}}\mathrm{APSP}
\quad\land\quad
\mathrm{APSP}\le_{\mathrm{sc}}\mathrm{TED}.
\]
The alphabet and the nonnegative integer edit-cost table are part of a TED input, and the alphabet may grow with the trees. The size parameter is the larger tree's node count for TED and the vertex count for APSP; weight bit length is an additional parameter. This general weighted interpretation is explicit: the imported survey's mention of a fixed alphabet does not match the APSP hardness theorem it cites. The general variant stated here was resolved affirmatively in 2025 and is retained as an inactive historical record.
why: The equivalence places a central comparison problem for hierarchical data in the same fine-grained complexity class as all-pairs shortest paths. It explains why a polynomial improvement over cubic time for either general weighted problem would transfer to the other, linking tree comparison to a foundational barrier in graph algorithms.
status_note: Resolved for the general weighted ordered-tree variant stated here: Nogler et al., STOC 2025 (inspected arXiv:2411.06502v3, 31 March 2025), prove the missing reduction to min-plus multiplication/APSP, complementing Bringmann et al.'s reverse direction. A bounded review through 16 September 2026 checked the definitions, main statements and selected proof-chain dependencies, and found no correcting or retracting primary result. It was not an independent verification of every lemma and is not a Lean verification. The survey's literal fixed-alphabet phrase is not covered by this resolution claim; its cited hardness theorem requires a growing alphabet.

sentences: Weighted ordered tree edit distance finds the minimum cost of a structure-preserving partial matching between two labeled rooted trees.
This historical question asks for deterministic subcubic reductions in both directions between general weighted tree edit distance and all-pairs shortest paths.
Its alphabet and edit-cost table are input data, and weight bit length is explicitly included in the running-time convention.

The reverse hardness direction and the STOC 2025 upper reduction together establish the general weighted equivalence, explaining how sufficiently fast algorithms transfer between tree comparison and shortest paths.
The record is archived as resolved while preserving the survey's conflicting fixed-alphabet wording and making no resolution claim for that restricted variant.

definitions:
A rooted ordered tree is a finite nonempty tree with one distinguished root and a linear order on each node's children. A proper ancestor of a node lies strictly above it on the path from the root. Preorder visits a node first and then visits its child subtrees in the prescribed order. For two incomparable nodes, “left of” means earlier in this preorder.

A TED input consists of two such trees \(T,T'\), with \(N,N'\) nodes, labels from \(\Sigma=\{1,\ldots,q\}\), and a table
\[
\kappa:(\Sigma\cup\{\bot\})^{2}\longrightarrow\mathbb N_{0}.
\]
Every symbol occurs in at least one input tree, so \(1\le q\le N+N'\); \(\bot\) is a separate deletion/insertion marker. Require \(\kappa(a,a)=0\) for every \(a\in\Sigma\cup\{\bot\}\). No symmetry or triangle inequality is required. The table specifies deletion \(\kappa(a,\bot)\), insertion \(\kappa(\bot,b)\), and a single relabeling \(\kappa(a,b)\).

An admissible edit mapping is a set \(M\subseteq V(T)\times V(T')\) in which no node appears in two pairs. For any two distinct pairs \((u,u'),(v,v')\in M\), require that \(u\) is a proper ancestor of \(v\) if and only if \(u'\) is a proper ancestor of \(v'\), and impose the same equivalence with \(u,v\) exchanged. For incomparable \(u,v\), require that \(u\) is left of \(v\) if and only if \(u'\) is left of \(v'\). Write \(D(M)\) and \(R(M)\) for the nodes appearing in the first and second coordinates. If \(\lambda,\lambda'\) are the node labels, the required exact scalar output is
\[
\operatorname{TED}(T,T',\kappa)=
\min_{M}
\left[
\sum_{(u,v)\in M}\kappa(\lambda(u),\lambda'(v))
+\sum_{u\in V(T)\setminus D(M)}\kappa(\lambda(u),\bot)
+\sum_{v\in V(T')\setminus R(M)}\kappa(\bot,\lambda'(v))
\right].
\]
The empty mapping is permitted. Roots need not be matched. This mapping formula is the definition, including for nonmetric tables; it does not permit arbitrarily many successive relabelings of the same node.

An APSP input is a directed graph on \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\), specified by an \(N\times N\) matrix whose entries are integer edge weights or an absent-edge marker. There is at most one edge per ordered pair. The promise is that no directed cycle has negative total weight. The required output is the full matrix of minimum path weights for all ordered vertex pairs, using \(+\infty\) for an unreachable pair and allowing a zero-length path from each vertex to itself. Path weight is the sum of its edge weights.

For either problem let \(n=\max\{2,N,N'\}\) for TED and \(n=\max\{2,N\}\) for APSP. Set
\[
L=\max\left(\{1\}\cup
\{\lceil\log_{2}(|z|+2)\rceil:z\text{ is a finite input weight}\}\right).
\]
Thus weights are binary integers of explicitly accounted bit length, rather than real numbers supplied with free arbitrary-precision arithmetic. In the usual regime \(|z|\le n^{b}\) for a fixed \(b\), one has \(L=O(\log n)\).

Fix the following encoding. For a nonnegative integer \(r\), let \(\ell\) be the length of the ordinary binary representation of \(r+1\), and encode \(r\) as \(\ell\) one-bits, one zero-bit, and those \(\ell\) binary bits. Encode a signed integer \(z\) by this code applied to \(2z\) if \(z\ge0\), and to \(-2z-1\) otherwise. A tree has nodes numbered in preorder and is represented by its size and an array of parent numbers and labels in node order, using parent zero for the root. Children are ordered by increasing node number, and a valid encoding must have the declared preorder. A TED payload gives \(N,N',q\), the two parent-and-label arrays, and the \((q+1)\times(q+1)\) table in row order, with \(\bot\) indexed zero; natural numbers use the code just defined. An APSP payload gives \(N\), then its matrix in row order; each entry has a presence bit and, when present, a signed integer code. Its output uses the analogous matrix encoding, with an absence bit representing \(+\infty\). TED outputs one nonnegative integer code. Both input types prefix their payload with the correctly calculated \(n,L\), encoded in that order as natural numbers. They have \(O(n\log(n+2)+n^{2}(L+1))\) bits.

Computations use uniform deterministic word-RAM programs with a fixed finite instruction list and finitely many registers. For a program there is a fixed integer \(a\ge1\), independent of its input, giving word width \(w=\lceil a\log_{2}(n+L+2)\rceil\). Memory cells have addresses and contents in \(\{0,\ldots,2^{w}-1\}\), and all cells outside the packed binary input are initially zero. The parameters \(n,L\) are also supplied in two initial registers. Allowed unit-cost instructions are register copy, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), unsigned integer division and remainder, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, unsigned comparison and conditional branch, reading or writing one addressed memory word, and appending one output bit. Division or remainder by zero returns zero; a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Larger integers are represented by multiple words and their processing is charged through these instructions. Programs must fit all memory addresses into words. There is no advice, random input or non-oracle external operation. Initialization, parsing, query construction, answer processing and output writing count toward running time.

Here is the reduction relation, with weight processing kept explicit. Put \(E=\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)\). A reduction program \(R\) has an additional exact oracle for a target problem \(Q\); it may submit a finite encoded valid \(Q\)-instance and obtain its encoded answer. Queries may depend on earlier answers. Query construction and answer reading use ordinary instructions; the oracle invocation itself costs one additional step. Let \(t_{R}(I)\) count these non-oracle instructions and invocations. If the successive queries have parameters \(n_{j},L_{j}\), define the charged cost
\[
B_{\varepsilon,c}(R,I)=t_{R}(I)+
\sum_{j}n_{j}^{\,3-\varepsilon}(L_{j}+1)^{c}.
\]
For \(\varepsilon,\delta\in E\), \(c,k\in\mathbb N_{0}\), \(C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), write \(S(P,Q;\varepsilon,c,\delta,k,C,R,I)\) when \(R\), using the exact \(Q\) oracle, makes only valid queries, halts with the exact required \(P\) output on the valid \(P\)-instance \(I\), and
\[
B_{\varepsilon,c}(R,I)\le Cn(I)^{\,3-\delta}(L(I)+1)^{k}.
\]
If it fails to halt or makes an invalid query, \(S\) is false. Define
\[
P\le_{\mathrm{sc}}Q
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall\varepsilon\in E\ \forall c\in\mathbb N_{0}\
\exists\delta\in E\ \exists k\in\mathbb N_{0}\
\exists C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists R\
\forall I\in\operatorname{Inst}(P)\
S(P,Q;\varepsilon,c,\delta,k,C,R,I).
\]
Here \(\operatorname{Inst}(P)\) is exactly the valid input set defined above. Each \(R\), including its word-width constant, is one finite program for all \(n,L\), not a separate program for each input length. The reduction program and constants may depend on \(\varepsilon,c\), but not on \(I\). This is a reduction requirement, stronger than merely asserting that the two problems happen to have the same yes-or-no answer to the existence of a fast algorithm. A hypothetical \(n^{3-\varepsilon}(L+1)^{c}\)-time oracle algorithm gives a \(n^{3-\delta}(L+1)^{k}\)-time source algorithm; \(\delta\) need not equal \(\varepsilon\).
answer_criterion:
The historical affirmative target requires a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of both displayed reduction statements, with correctness on every valid instance, the two charged-cost bounds and the stipulated uniform deterministic model. A complete Lean proof of the full logical negation would instead have to establish that for at least one ordered pair
\[
(P,Q)\in\{(\mathrm{TED},\mathrm{APSP}),(\mathrm{APSP},\mathrm{TED})\}
\]
there exist \(\varepsilon\in E\) and \(c\in\mathbb N_{0}\) such that
\[
\forall\delta\in E\ \forall k\in\mathbb N_{0}\
\forall C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall R\
\exists I\in\operatorname{Inst}(P)\
\neg S(P,Q;\varepsilon,c,\delta,k,C,R,I).
\]
This negation quantifies over every eligible reduction program and every uniform bound; failure of one proposed reduction is insufficient. A reduction for only unweighted costs, only a fixed alphabet, or only one direction does not alone meet the target. This archived record does not assert that a Lean formalization of the published affirmative result has already been supplied.

context_blocks.text: The 2018 survey poses APSP equivalence for tree edit distance in Section 5. Its description includes a fixed alphabet, whereas its cited hardness paper proves APSP hardness using an alphabet growing linearly with tree size. The present record explicitly recovers the general weighted variant from that cited result and preserves this source discrepancy.

Bringmann, Gawrychowski, Mozes and Weimann establish the hardness direction for general weighted ordered trees. Their separate constant-alphabet result assumes a stronger maximum-weight clique conjecture. It does not supply the missing APSP hardness direction for a fixed alphabet.

Nogler, Polak, Saha, Vassilevska Williams, Xu and Ye establish the converse reduction in their STOC 2025 paper. Combined with the earlier hardness result, it resolves the general weighted equivalence. Their bound also yields a subpolynomial-factor improvement over cubic time; that is distinct from an exponent improvement by a fixed positive constant.

The reduction convention permits polynomial dependence on weight bit length. The deterministic triangle/matrix equivalences provide this dependence without requiring the optional randomized variant that removes it. The unweighted TED algorithms in the 2025 paper concern a different cost restriction.

checked_sources: Read the active canonical card and docs/RULES.md. The imported title and formal question are generic; no fixed alphabet, weights or computational model had been specified. The original textbook notes are to remain verbatim. Recovering the general weighted variant is an explicitly documented interpretation grounded in the survey's own hardness reference and the 2025 resolution, not a proof of the survey's literal fixed-alphabet variant.

Read the 2018 survey's Section 5 p. 14 and reference [44]. Its fixed-alphabet wording conflicts with the actual scope of BGMW Theorem 1. Correct the current locator from Section 4 to Section 5, but preserve the old import locator as historical provenance.

Read BGMW arXiv v1 definitions, Theorem 1, Section 2, Lemma 2, Theorem 2 and the beginning of Section 3. Lemma 2 produces O(n)-node trees with O(n) distinct labels and a quadratic explicit cost table from a weighted graph. The displayed matching costs have polynomial magnitude when source weights do; Theorem 2 recovers the minimum triangle weight by an additive adjustment. The Section 3 constant-alphabet result uses a different, stronger clique conjecture. This is a bounded check of the APSP branch, not an audit of the entire constant-alphabet construction.

Checked the mapping convention carefully. BGMW subtracts unmatched-node costs before giving possibly negative adjusted matching costs and infinite forbidden costs. These need not become negative original edit prices: with distinct node labels, choose an integer K larger than all absolute finite adjusted costs, use insertion/deletion K and substitution 2K plus the adjusted cost. A forbidden pair can receive substitution 2K, because removing a zero-benefit pair preserves admissibility and cannot worsen the optimum. All resulting prices are finite nonnegative integers of polynomial magnitude for polynomial source weights. This normalization is an explicit audit deduction; it is not quoted as a separate theorem or offered as a solver hint in the public definitions.

Read the 2025 v3 Main Theorem 1, Section 2.1, Lemma 2.1 and Main Theorem 3, Corollary 5.5, Section 5.2, Theorem 5.18 and Section 6. The mapping constraints coincide with those used for the hardness direction. The weighted theorem permits a growing alphabet and arbitrary supplied weights, and its addition/comparison computations on integer scores have polynomial overhead in bit length. Section 5.2 explains the required input subproblems; Section 6 formally gives TED-to-SED through Lemmas 6.3 and 6.4, notwithstanding its reversed-looking section title. The read-through checked the dependency chain, not every auxiliary lemma in Sections 4–5.

For the equal-size case needed here, the weighted theorem gives min-plus time plus an n^{2+o(1)} term and logarithmic reduction overhead. Its unbalanced result is stronger and is not an extra demand of this card. Its advertised n^3/2^{Omega(sqrt(log n))} corollary is not a truly subcubic exponent bound. The only explicitly randomized multiplication subroutine in the inspected weighted/unweighted discussion is used for the separate bounded-monotone unweighted result; the general weighted reduction makes deterministic decomposition and arithmetic operations.

Downloaded the author-hosted full JACM 2018 bridge manuscript. Definition 3.1 is an actual oracle-query budget definition, rather than a bare equivalence of algorithm-existence propositions. Theorem 4.2 and Lemma 4.2 use deterministic partitions and simultaneous binary search, with logarithmic integer-universe overhead. The separate Section 4.3 random permutation removes that universe dependence and is unnecessary here. The explicit L-parameter convention records polynomial bit overhead even for small oracle instances whose values still depend on the original input.
